extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, film & television writers, and story analysts/students of narrative craft
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical criteria for designing dramatic story and scenes for film/television: how to choose and compose events, define scenes, create value-charged change through conflict, and balance imaginative and sensory powers while applying craft and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The sign on the door reads 'Story Department.' A good story makes a good film possible; failure to make the story work virtually guarantees disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story is the organizing imperative: dialogue and description, however well-written, cannot rescue a lifeless story. Prioritize story problems (lack of progression, weak motivation, no discernible protagonist, unrelated tensions, empty subtext, holes) over surface craft issues when evaluating a screenplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common story problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of progression, false motivation, redundant characters, empty subtext, holes and other such story problems are the root causes of a bland, boring text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a script, look specifically for progression of action, believable motivation for choices, purposeful characters (no redundancies), meaningful subtext, and closure/consistency (no holes). Scenes or beats that exist only to convey information or wallpaper should be reworked or removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define characters' desires and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the total creative effort, most goes into designing story: Who are these characters? What do they want? Why do they want it? How do they go about getting it? What stops them? What are the consequences?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete story design answers these questions; failure to specify desires, motivations, tactics, obstacles, and consequences leads to weak or aimless storytelling. Use these questions as a checklist when crafting or evaluating a premise or outline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master craft to engage and reward audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft is the concert of techniques by which we create a conspiracy of interest between ourselves and the audience, to draw the audience into deep involvement, hold that involvement, and ultimately reward it with a moving and meaningful experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft includes structural choices, pacing, scene design, and the orchestration of revelations. The writer must consciously apply craft (write, read, analyze, rewrite) to free the subconscious and achieve emotional and intellectual payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance literary talent and story talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary talent is the creative conversion of ordinary language into expressive form; story talent is the conversion of life into more powerful, meaningful experience. Story talent is primary; literary talent is secondary but essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work converts life into story (story talent) rather than merely showing nicely written surface detail. Beautiful prose cannot substitute for the ability to shape events into meaningful narrative. Cultivate craft to maximize both talents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the two failed extremes (portraiture and spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two persistent failed screenplay types: the 'personal story' understructured, slice-of-life portraiture that mistakes verisimilitude for truth; and the 'guaranteed commercial success' overstructured spectacle that substitutes kinesis for genuine human truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge stories by whether they abstract and reveal Big 'T' Truth beyond mere facts or visual thrills. Portraiture often lacks deeper conflict and motivated change; spectacle often lacks meaningful relation to life. Strong stories balance imagination and sense-perception and ground spectacle in human truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as metaphor for life
rubrics_metrics.description: A storyteller is a life poet who transforms day-to-day living, inner and outer life, dream and actuality into a poem whose rhyme scheme is events rather than words—a metaphor that says: Life is like this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the story abstracts life to discover essences without becoming an abstraction that loses lived credibility. The writer's task is to find the meaning (truth) behind facts, not merely to record occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance sensory perception and imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers of portraiture often have the power of the senses; writers of spectacle often have the power of imagination. Strong storytelling strikes a balance along the spectrum between fact and imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the writer uses both sensory detail and imaginative invention in harmony. Excess on either end (pure reportage or pure fantasy/spectacle) weakens a story's emotional and thematic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure as selection and composition of events
rubrics_metrics.description: STRUCTURE is a selection of events from the characters' life stories that is composed into a strategic sequence to arouse specific emotions and to express a specific view of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging structure, ask: which events were chosen, in what order, and to what purpose? Events should be composed intentionally to elicit targeted emotional responses and to convey the writer's thematic point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event = meaningful change in terms of value
rubrics_metrics.description: A STORY EVENT creates meaningful change in the life situation of a character that is expressed and experienced in terms of a VALUE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate events by whether they change a character's condition with respect to a clear story value (alive/dead, love/hate, freedom/slavery, hope/despair, etc.). Trivial or purely circumstantial changes are not story events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events must be achieved through conflict (not mere coincidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Story Event creates meaningful change in the life situation of a character ... and ACHIEVED THROUGH CONFLICT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discount events that occur solely by chance. For an event to be powerful and narratively satisfying, it must arise from character choices and conflicts—inner, interpersonal, social, or environmental—so the change feels motivated and earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Values (use reversible value-charges)
rubrics_metrics.description: STORY VALUES are the universal qualities of human experience that may shift from positive to negative, or negative to positive, from one moment to the next (e.g., alive/dead, love/hate, truth/lie, courage/cowardice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing scenes and events, identify the value at stake and map its charge at scene opening and closing. Values should be capable of reversal to create dramatic tension and meaningful change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene definition and ideal: each scene should be a Story Event
rubrics_metrics.description: A SCENE is an action through conflict in more or less continuous time and space that turns the value-charged condition of a character's life on at least one value with a degree of perceptible significance. Ideally every scene is a STORY EVENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess scenes by asking: What value is at stake at the top? Where is that value at the close? If nothing changes, the scene is a nonevent and likely expendable. Aim to make each scene enact a value-turn through conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut exposition scenes that don't turn
rubrics_metrics.description: If the value-charged condition of the character's life stays unchanged from one end of a scene to the other, nothing meaningful happens. If exposition is a scene's sole justification, a disciplined writer will trash it and weave its information into the film elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a pruning rule in revision: identify scenes that merely present background, history, or context without enacting conflict-driven change; rework or remove them and distribute necessary information into active scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: No scene that doesn't turn (the Turn Principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: No scene that doesn't turn. We work to round every scene from beginning to end by turning a value at stake in a character's life from the positive to the negative or the negative to the positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This universal principle applies across genres (action genres often turn on public values; education/psychological genres on interior values). Use the turn as a focusing device when structuring beats and sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical scene count for feature films
rubrics_metrics.description: For a typical film, the writer will choose forty to sixty Story Events or, as they're commonly known, scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this guideline when planning pacing and scope: features often concentrate on 40–60 meaningful scenes; novels/playwrights may vary. The guideline helps estimate momentum and the density of events necessary to sustain the film's length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work cycle: write, read, analyze, rewrite
rubrics_metrics.description: What's the rhythm of a writer's day? You enter your imagined world and write; you step out and read what you've written; you analyze: 'Is it good? Does it work? Why not? Should I cut? Add? Reorder?' You write, you read; create, critique; re-imagine, rewrite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the quality of rewriting: craft and revision are necessary to correct imperfections and achieve the intended emotional and thematic effects. A writer should be able to diagnose weaknesses and apply craft to fix them rather than rely on impulse alone.
